story_text.value:
Most stock charts work in a similar way - they give you a bunch of tools to draw lines and patterns on a chart. This is fine, and I assume that advanced traders enjoy drawing on the chart. But it's also annoying, and seems arbitrary sometimes.

So I created stock charts that annotate themselves. The process has two stages:

First, the algorithm goes through the daily candles and identifies the structure: support and resistance zones, trendlines, volume spikes, etc.

Then, an LLM models understands the relative importance of the structure components, decides which ones to include, and annotates them.

Finally, it lays out the possible future moves: base case, bull and bear cases.

It's included in Portfolio Genius, the AI investment manager I'm building, and it's available free without signup here: https://portfoliogenius.ai/features/ai-annotated-charts

story_text.value:
Guys - OpenAI Decisions, Jev, World Models are interesting.

We ran some tests for the C-suite to decide between OpenAI Decisions vs. their own existing models vs. training their proprietary Financial World Model. Sharing the results of our sample tests.

If you like a walkthrough with video of results - see this video - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UN1LIF01uHQ

We are also trying to reach OpenAI team & community to collaborate on running various tests to help the C-suite to make decisions. Which involves which business cases, they wish to map on which Decision models.

Summary: Small Financial World Model compared to OpenAI Decisions.

This test is not to build a better model. But to help C-suites make informed choices. There are various considerations viz

Latency Cost per decision On-premises or Hosted APIs Regulatory & Compliance Mapping to use cases Financial modelling or LLM-based reasoning as underlying architecture We ran tests to:

Predict credit defaults Cross-sell propensity Churn Risk Future cash flows Future state of customers & causal impacts of interventions like no-action, Payment reminders etc.

These tests are specific to banking use cases.

Why Benchmark & comparison:

Small on-prem Decision Models are needed due to latency, cost, regulatory or protecting the proprietary data for Enterprises.

This benchmarking helps C-suite executives to decide which option - their in-house models or other options are better. Vaayu FinBench also includes some specific banking-related business cases as examples.

World Model also has action-conditioning. Thus, it predicts which decision optimizes the future outcomes. Eg Risk weighted return or prevent default. Core ask from Banks

Small Financial World Model is trained on-premesis on proprietary data for enterprises.

Scope - This is only for demonstration purposes to give a glimpse of how to compare various options. The dataset & model size is way too small yet. On a larger proprietary dataset, the results need to be benchmarked.

Results: Latency - A co-located Small Financial World Model way improves latency. Major part may be coming due to network latency. So this is one area where we would like to discuss alternatives with OpenAI team & community. Is there a smaller on-premesis version for Decision Model avaialble for co-location.

Credit Defaults - Our Small Financial World model worked worse than Decision API.

Cash Churn & Cross Sell propensity - Our Small Financial World model improved marginally. It’s obvious that since Decision API hasnt seen the propreitary data. The marginal improvement shows model is learning..but our model is very very small (Few 100 thousand parameters) trained on small dataset.. But test demonstrates - architecture is capable of learning better.

Action conditions outcomes - This is available in World Model …but we aren’t aware of this in Decision API yet.

Financial Modelling - Model is trained finance native can handle temporal & causal scenarios

If you like a walkthrough - see this video - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UN1LIF01uHQ

Disclaimer: This is quick tests results & has some know issues. This is only for demonstration purpose. We have included OpenAI Decisions for now...Including Jev in next releases. At the moment talking to C-suite & Banks for what they wish.

We find Decision API & World Models interesting developments especially in finance & enterprises space. Looking forward to collaborate with OpenAI team & community how to enable C-suite to make choices…which are underway right now at enterprises.

story_text.value:
Hello HN, I'm Nik. I built Infinity for myself because I tend to love to rabbit-hole on various subjects.

I usually have 3-4 windows open for ChatGPT desktop + Claude + Ollama. Typically, I'd ask a question, see something interesting in the answer, and then keep expanding on it. The mental chain of thought eventually gets lost and I would start from scratch again. Second, I also wanted to compare answers across multiple models. From there, pick and use the best one and continue.

So I built Infinity for myself. Multiple windows, multiple chats. Projects all aligned in one place. But the best part is when you start highlighting any part of the response - you can branch off and fork into new chat sessions from there without losing your original chain of thought.

It's a native Mac app written in Swift. You can use all the popular cloud models that you already pay for but on top of that, you can use local models as well. You can even set out what each model's job is and assign certain models for certain jobs.

It's free, there's no account, no analytics on the actual app. Everything is stored locally. Just download, connect up, and get going.

Still extremely early but if there is interest, would love to hear what works and what doesn't!

story_text.value:
I built a pay-as-you-go two star hotel for bots that you’re only charged for while it’s active. Typically wakes in under a second, runs on a vm, and costs very little while it’s paused.

In my free time I’ve been building a firecracker based vm orchestration platform. In order to dogfood the thing I put together a place to run agent harnesses (openclaw etc) on machines but only pay for them when they are in use. What started as a demo has grown legs into a more unique product than the platform.

Botel has prebaked templates for each harness, with a daemon of mine running beside it monitoring the harness’ activity. It communicates out to the host over a link-local self api; instructing when to pause or wake next based on stored schedules. With a proxy in front to wake on http. The harnesses are preconfigured to point to my llm gateway that proxies through to openrouter.

One of the biggest struggles while building it was preventing claude from going off the rails with hotel metaphors in the ui. Once it sees a joke it really strangles the hell out of it.

A more real ;) awkward part is that the harnesses don’t expose exactly what I needed in order to detect activity. I'm still struggling with how to handle the fact that background job can be short or long lived (http/dev servers etc). I’m hoping to propose changes to hermes, openclaw, and dsh soon for a consistent way to know what kind of a job is running with annotated lifecycle hooks.

Some of the nicest things about the bot hotel are:

- You get a proper linux vm with sudo, so you can ssh in, scp, or run docker.

- You can ask the agent to expose something publicly or privately (behind your login). A port gets a unique hostname/url. Those endpoints also wake the vm. So you could build and host a little app or self host something.

- Guided telegram setup. It’s pretty awkward in general/my setup hopefully takes some of the edge off.

A friend of mine who built a website for his local orienteering club has used this to make it easy for peoge on the committee to update news and events. All in all it should cost something like 40 cents a month to run so long as the club members don’t get too friendly with the agent.

If you’re interested, give the thing a spin. The first 50 signups get $2 credit. Price is pretty low at 3c per GB of ram per hour awake, plus a few cents per GB-month asleep. You use credit for inference or byok.

Let me know how you get on and whether you have any ideas or requests for it. Thx!

story_text.value:
hey hn, sven from Reason Machines (YC F26).

we've been experimenting with how fast we can push our ci/cd and code storage systems when swarms of coding agents are all pushing at once. turns out giving 100 agents git push basically ddos'es normal git servers.

so we wrote aspen: an open-source git server (apache 2.0) that hits 567 pushes/sec on a single 8-core box with stock git clients.

to stress test it live, we put up a shared canvas where every pixel is a real git push: https://place.reasonmachines.com

code & how it works: - blog: https://reasonmachines.com/blog/aspen - github: https://github.com/reason-machines/aspen

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I’m Jan. I am co-author of the Agentic Identity Broker (AIB), an MIT-licensed OAuth2 broker in the Zalando Incubator, that lets a user give an AI agent scoped, revocable access to MCP services.

The broker solves three major challenges that are especially relevant in corporate environments: (A) Enable users to delegate workloads to agents without providing the agents all the user’s tokens. (B) Connect fragmented identity and authorization systems. (C) Centralize tool approvals and audit logging.

We built AIB to fill an infrastructure gap in our own agent platform. At this moment in time, IETF working groups are still finalizing standards for agent identity, and vendors are still turning the necessary infrastructure into off-the-shelf products. We needed that infrastructure today.

How it works: the user consents once per agent and service. The broker stores the third-party tokens encrypted. At request time a gateway (e.g. Agentgateway) does RFC 8693 token exchange. Agents never see user tokens and MCP servers only implement tools and don’t need to care about all the OAuth 2.1 plumbing.

AIB is v0.1 and runs in production, bringing together hundreds of our agents with dozens of internal and external MCP servers.

To try it locally: clone the repo, run "just compose-up-detached".

The current features focus on on-behalf-of (OBO) use cases, where human actors delegate to agents. Next we are looking to also support headless agents, where agents are invoked by machines. Intent-based authorization is yet another package on our roadmap. If you’ve built either, or have feedback on the UI/UX, I’d like to hear from you!

story_text.value:
Hi HN, my friend's team and I have been building a game called GRID, a dog poker game with an AI twist.

Under the cute dog graphics, GRID is an arena where LLMs compete, with no-limit hold’em as the medium. You duke it out as a strategist, vibe coder, and bot maker.

Why: models get compared on benchmarks all the time, but rarely as my agent against yours in its truest form. GRID is our attempt at creating that arena, because we believe this type of game will exist in the future, as AI becomes as common a tool as the browser.

How it works:

* Paste a prompt and an MCP config into Claude Code, Codex or any MCP client. The agent waits for its turn and sends actions back through tool calls.

* The strategy is text written in the game, up to 6,000 characters. We thought it’d be cool to have a preset, “Play like Elon”, to show you what you can do.

* You can change the strategy any time, and it applies from the next action. You can even ask your AI to change it for you, based on what it learns about its opponents’ strategies from the match history.

* Free beta. Play chips only. We just opened up the game today and are gathering data on how to steer this ship next.

Rough edges:

* MCP can be finicky, especially if you refresh your browser while in a match. If this happens and you can’t get your agent to connect, wait 5 min and retry | log out using the settings button at the top left and log back in. Stability is currently our top priority.

* MCP also uses a lot of tokens, more than the game should, because every tool call costs tokens. We plan to overhaul this with a new connection type in a future version so it’s much more efficient.

* There’s a built-in local model for folks who don’t want to use their own AI. It plays basic hold’em OK but struggles to follow written strategies. If you want to try it, I’d recommend leaving your strategy blank. Sadly, it plays best with no instructions.

* House bots fill empty seats. We made this choice so matches happen even when only a few people are online.

Honestly, I’m most curious how you’d write a strategy that holds up against everyone else’s agents. And if MCP setup breaks on you, please tell me. We'll be in the thread as long as possible.

story_text.value:
I travel with friends a lot and we used to always use Splitwise to settle our group's expenses, but over the years I've grown so frustrated with its user experience how bad it is for entering anything more complex than an evenly split bill.

So I though I could surely do better. I mean, how hard could it be?

That was 4 years ago and it's been my pet project for quite some time. It never felt close to done, but recently - admittedly with lots of AI help - I've managed to polish it enough to call it ready. We've already used it with our group and now I'm putting it out here hoping some of you will find it useful too.
